publications.name: Progressive Taxation and Dynamic Wealth Inequality under Luxury Saving
publications.summary: Progressive Taxation and Dynamic Wealth Inequality under Luxury Saving. When the rich save a rising share of their wealth, a tax can compress the distribution at every date and still leave the sequence pulling apart. The classical characterizations hold within a period. Across periods they have no counterpart. What governs the trajectory is whether a second levy on accumulated wealth takes back what accumulation spread apart. An income tax never does. A wealth tax can, and I give an example where it compresses at both dates while the sequence diverges anyway.

publications.name: The Myth of the Informed Voter
publications.summary: The Myth of the Informed Voter. Campaign money buys attention, not information. Even when voters are fully informed, the election turns on which issues a campaign makes salient: with spending unbounded, the loudest issue becomes decisive and its owner wins however narrow her support elsewhere. A binding cap keeps any issue from commanding a majority of attention and leaves the election settled across many, though whether that seats the broadly representative candidate depends on the electorate.

publications.name: Progressive Taxation and Wealth Inequality with Forward-Looking Savers
publications.summary: Progressive Taxation and Wealth Inequality with Forward-Looking Savers. A dynamic extension with forward-looking agents. The question is whether the non-convergence result depends on myopia. It does not. Agents who anticipate the returns to accumulation save harder still. Containing the divergence then takes marginal-rate progressivity, a stricter standard than average-rate.
